Which functions are kernels?

So far we started from an embedding and computed its kernel. In practice you often go the other way: you dream up a similarity function K:X×X→RK: \mathcal X \times \mathcal X \to \mathbb RK:X×X→R that encodes your prior knowledge, and you want to know whether some embedding stands behind it. If none does, the whole derivation above, which needed K(x,x′)=⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩K(x, x') = \langle \psi(x), \psi(x') \rangleK(x,x′)=⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩, collapses. Is there a test you can run on KKK alone?

There is, and it is about Gram matrices. A symmetric m×mm \times mm×m matrix GGG is positive semidefinite when α⊤Gα=∑i,jαiαjGi,j≥0\boldsymbol\alpha^\top G \boldsymbol\alpha = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j G_{i,j} \ge 0α⊤Gα=∑i,j​αi​αj​Gi,j​≥0 for every α∈Rm\boldsymbol\alpha \in \mathbb R^mα∈Rm. A symmetric function KKK is positive semidefinite when every Gram matrix it produces is: for every mmm and every x1,…,xm∈Xx_1, \dots, x_m \in \mathcal Xx1​,…,xm​∈X, the matrix Gi,j=K(xi,xj)G_{i,j} = K(x_i, x_j)Gi,j​=K(xi​,xj​) is positive semidefinite. The quadratic form α⊤Gα\boldsymbol\alpha^\top G \boldsymbol\alphaα⊤Gα is the double sum we met as ∥w∥2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥w∥2: pick a weight αi\alpha_iαi​ per point and add αiαjGi,j\alpha_i \alpha_j G_{i,j}αi​αj​Gi,j​ over all pairs. In plain words: no choice of weights makes the double sum negative. The function quad in the snippet below is this sum, term by term.

Characterization of kernels. A symmetric function K:X×X→RK: \mathcal X \times \mathcal X \to \mathbb RK:X×X→R is the inner product of some embedding into a Hilbert space if and only if it is positive semidefinite.

Before the proof, let’s see the test bite. On the points 1 and 2 of the real line, try the product K(x,x′)=xx′K(x, x') = x x'K(x,x′)=xx′, which is plainly an inner product in R1\mathbb R^1R1, and the maximum K(x,x′)=max⁡{x,x′}K(x, x') = \max\{x, x'\}K(x,x′)=max{x,x′}, which looks like a harmless similarity:

import random

def quad(G, a):
    n = len(a)
    return sum(a[i] * G[i][j] * a[j]
               for i in range(n) for j in range(n))

pts = [1, 2]
for name, K in (("product", lambda p, q: p * q), ("max", max)):
    G = [[K(p, q) for q in pts] for p in pts]
    print(name, G, quad(G, [1, -1]))

rng = random.Random(0)
xs = [[rng.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(3)] for _ in range(6)]
G = [[(1 + sum(a * b for a, b in zip(p, q))) ** 2 for q in xs]
     for p in xs]
worst = min(quad(G, [rng.gauss(0, 1) for _ in xs])
            for _ in range(10_000))
print(worst >= 0)

It prints product [[1, 2], [2, 4]] 1, then max [[1, 2], [2, 2]] -1, then True. The maximum fails on just two points: α=(1,−1)\boldsymbol\alpha = (1, -1)α=(1,−1) gives 1−2−2+2=−1<01 - 2 - 2 + 2 = -1 < 01−2−2+2=−1<0, so by the theorem no embedding has max⁡\maxmax as its inner product, however clever. The degree-2 polynomial kernel, on six random points in R3\mathbb R^3R3, survives 10,000 random α\boldsymbol\alphaα (a spot check, not a proof; the proof is the polynomial-kernel computation above together with the easy direction below).

[diagram:gram: built on the lesson page]

Proof, the easy direction. Suppose K(x,x′)=⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩K(x, x') = \langle \psi(x), \psi(x') \rangleK(x,x′)=⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩. Then KKK is symmetric because the inner product is. Fix points x1,…,xmx_1, \dots, x_mx1​,…,xm​ and any α\boldsymbol\alphaα. Using bilinearity to pull the sums inside,

α⊤Gα=∑i,jαiαj⟨ψ(xi),ψ(xj)⟩=⟨∑iαiψ(xi),∑jαjψ(xj)⟩=∥∑iαiψ(xi)∥2≥0.\boldsymbol\alpha^\top G \boldsymbol\alpha = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j \langle \psi(x_i), \psi(x_j) \rangle = \Big\langle \sum_i \alpha_i \psi(x_i), \sum_j \alpha_j \psi(x_j) \Big\rangle = \Big\| \sum_i \alpha_i \psi(x_i) \Big\|^2 \ge 0.α⊤Gα=i,j∑​αi​αj​⟨ψ(xi​),ψ(xj​)⟩=⟨i∑​αi​ψ(xi​),j∑​αj​ψ(xj​)⟩=​i∑​αi​ψ(xi​)​2≥0.

In plain words: the double sum is the squared length of a vector, and squared lengths are never negative. For the product kernel on 1 and 2 with α=(1,−1)\boldsymbol\alpha = (1, -1)α=(1,−1), the vector is 1−2=−11 - 2 = -11−2=−1, and its square is the 1 printed above.

Proof, the interesting direction. Now suppose KKK is symmetric and positive semidefinite. We have to invent a space and an embedding. The idea is bold: let each point be represented by its own row of similarities. For x∈Xx \in \mathcal Xx∈X, let ψ(x)\psi(x)ψ(x) be the function K(⋅,x)K(\cdot, x)K(⋅,x) (the dot marks the empty slot), which sends x′x'x′ to K(x′,x)K(x', x)K(x′,x). These are elements of the vector space of all functions from X\mathcal XX to R\mathbb RR. Let VVV be the set of their finite linear combinations, functions of the form f=∑iαiK(⋅,xi)f = \sum_i \alpha_i K(\cdot, x_i)f=∑i​αi​K(⋅,xi​).

On VVV, define

⟨∑iαiK(⋅,xi),  ∑jβjK(⋅,xj′)⟩=∑i,jαiβjK(xi,xj′).\Big\langle \sum_i \alpha_i K(\cdot, x_i), \; \sum_j \beta_j K(\cdot, x'_j) \Big\rangle = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \beta_j K(x_i, x'_j).⟨i∑​αi​K(⋅,xi​),j∑​βj​K(⋅,xj′​)⟩=i,j∑​αi​βj​K(xi​,xj′​).

In plain words: the inner product of two combinations is the kernel summed over every pair of their points, weighted by both coefficients. The function inner in the snippet at the end of this proof is this formula term by term. We must check four things: that this is well defined, symmetric, bilinear, and positive definite.

Well defined. A function in VVV can have many representations as a combination, so we must check that the formula does not depend on which one we pick. Write f=∑iαiK(⋅,xi)f = \sum_i \alpha_i K(\cdot, x_i)f=∑i​αi​K(⋅,xi​) and g=∑jβjK(⋅,xj′)g = \sum_j \beta_j K(\cdot, x'_j)g=∑j​βj​K(⋅,xj′​). Then f(xj′)=∑iαiK(xj′,xi)=∑iαiK(xi,xj′)f(x'_j) = \sum_i \alpha_i K(x'_j, x_i) = \sum_i \alpha_i K(x_i, x'_j)f(xj′​)=∑i​αi​K(xj′​,xi​)=∑i​αi​K(xi​,xj′​), using symmetry, so the formula equals ∑jβjf(xj′)\sum_j \beta_j f(x'_j)∑j​βj​f(xj′​). That expression depends on fff only through its values, not through the αi\alpha_iαi​ and xix_ixi​. By the same computation with the roles swapped, the formula also equals ∑iαig(xi)\sum_i \alpha_i g(x_i)∑i​αi​g(xi​), which depends on ggg only through its values. So the number is the same for every pair of representations.

Symmetric and bilinear. Swapping fff and ggg swaps the order inside K(xi,xj′)K(x_i, x'_j)K(xi​,xj′​), and KKK is symmetric. Linearity in each argument is immediate from the formula.

Positive definite. For f=∑iαiK(⋅,xi)f = \sum_i \alpha_i K(\cdot, x_i)f=∑i​αi​K(⋅,xi​), ⟨f,f⟩=∑i,jαiαjK(xi,xj)=α⊤Gα≥0\langle f, f \rangle = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j K(x_i, x_j) = \boldsymbol\alpha^\top G \boldsymbol\alpha \ge 0⟨f,f⟩=∑i,j​αi​αj​K(xi​,xj​)=α⊤Gα≥0, by the assumption on KKK. It remains to show that ⟨f,f⟩=0\langle f, f \rangle = 0⟨f,f⟩=0 forces f=0f = 0f=0. Two small facts do it. The first is the reproducing property: taking g=K(⋅,x)g = K(\cdot, x)g=K(⋅,x), a single term with coefficient 1, the formula gives

⟨f,K(⋅,x)⟩=∑iαiK(xi,x)=f(x).\langle f, K(\cdot, x) \rangle = \sum_i \alpha_i K(x_i, x) = f(x).⟨f,K(⋅,x)⟩=i∑​αi​K(xi​,x)=f(x).

In plain words: to evaluate fff at xxx, take its inner product with K(⋅,x)K(\cdot, x)K(⋅,x). The second is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality ∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤⟨f,f⟩⟨g,g⟩|\langle f, g \rangle| \le \sqrt{\langle f, f \rangle} \sqrt{\langle g, g \rangle}∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤⟨f,f⟩​⟨g,g⟩​, which holds for any symmetric bilinear form with ⟨h,h⟩≥0\langle h, h \rangle \ge 0⟨h,h⟩≥0. (For every real ttt, 0≤⟨f+tg,f+tg⟩=⟨f,f⟩+2t⟨f,g⟩+t2⟨g,g⟩0 \le \langle f + t g, f + t g \rangle = \langle f, f \rangle + 2t \langle f, g \rangle + t^2 \langle g, g \rangle0≤⟨f+tg,f+tg⟩=⟨f,f⟩+2t⟨f,g⟩+t2⟨g,g⟩. If ⟨g,g⟩>0\langle g, g \rangle > 0⟨g,g⟩>0, a quadratic in ttt that never goes negative has discriminant 4⟨f,g⟩2−4⟨f,f⟩⟨g,g⟩≤04\langle f, g \rangle^2 - 4 \langle f, f \rangle \langle g, g \rangle \le 04⟨f,g⟩2−4⟨f,f⟩⟨g,g⟩≤0. If ⟨g,g⟩=0\langle g, g \rangle = 0⟨g,g⟩=0, the expression is linear in ttt and stays nonnegative for all ttt only if ⟨f,g⟩=0\langle f, g \rangle = 0⟨f,g⟩=0.) Put them together:

∣f(x)∣=∣⟨f,K(⋅,x)⟩∣≤⟨f,f⟩K(x,x).|f(x)| = |\langle f, K(\cdot, x) \rangle| \le \sqrt{\langle f, f \rangle} \sqrt{K(x, x)}.∣f(x)∣=∣⟨f,K(⋅,x)⟩∣≤⟨f,f⟩​K(x,x)​.

So a function of length 0 is 0 everywhere. If ⟨f,f⟩=0\langle f, f \rangle = 0⟨f,f⟩=0, then f(x)=0f(x) = 0f(x)=0 for every xxx, so fff is the zero function.

So VVV is an inner product space, and by construction

⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩=⟨K(⋅,x),K(⋅,x′)⟩=K(x,x′).\langle \psi(x), \psi(x') \rangle = \langle K(\cdot, x), K(\cdot, x') \rangle = K(x, x').⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩=⟨K(⋅,x),K(⋅,x′)⟩=K(x,x′).

To be a Hilbert space in the strict sense, VVV must also be complete. The standard completion adds the limits of its Cauchy sequences, extends the inner product to them, and changes none of the values above. And nothing this lesson does needs more: the representer theorem only ever projects onto the span of mmm training vectors, where completeness is automatic. ■\blacksquare■

The reproducing property is worth seeing in numbers, because it is the whole trick in one line: evaluating a function in VVV is taking an inner product with K(⋅,x)K(\cdot, x)K(⋅,x). Here f=K(⋅,0)−2K(⋅,1)+0.5K(⋅,2.5)f = K(\cdot, 0) - 2K(\cdot, 1) + 0.5 K(\cdot, 2.5)f=K(⋅,0)−2K(⋅,1)+0.5K(⋅,2.5) for the Gaussian kernel with σ=1\sigma = 1σ=1:

import math

def K(x, xp):
    return math.exp(-(x - xp) ** 2 / 2)

centers, alpha = [0.0, 1.0, 2.5], [1.0, -2.0, 0.5]

def f(x):
    return sum(a * K(c, x) for a, c in zip(alpha, centers))

def inner(alpha, xs, beta, xps):
    return sum(a * b * K(x, xp) for a, x in zip(alpha, xs)
               for b, xp in zip(beta, xps))

x = 1.7
print(round(f(x), 10),
      round(inner(alpha, centers, [1.0], [x]), 10))
norm_f = math.sqrt(inner(alpha, centers, alpha, centers))
print(abs(f(x)) <= norm_f * math.sqrt(K(x, x)))

It prints -0.9665884814 -0.9665884814 and True: the value of fff at 1.7 equals its inner product with K(⋅,1.7)K(\cdot, 1.7)K(⋅,1.7), and the Cauchy–Schwarz bound from the proof holds.

Soft-SVM with kernels, trained by SGD

We could hand the α\boldsymbol\alphaα form of soft-SVM to a quadratic-programming solver. There is a simpler road, and it reuses something you already built. In lesson 15b you solved soft-SVM in the form

min⁡w  λ2∥w∥2+1m∑i=1mmax⁡{0,1−yi⟨w,xi⟩}\min_{\mathbf w} \; \frac{\lambda}{2} \|\mathbf w\|^2 + \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \max\{0, 1 - y_i \langle \mathbf w, \mathbf x_i \rangle\}wmin​2λ​∥w∥2+m1​i=1∑m​max{0,1−yi​⟨w,xi​⟩}

with SGD, lesson 14a’s stochastic gradient descent, which steps against the slope of one random example’s loss at a time. The λ2\frac{\lambda}{2}2λ​ is a convenience of SGD: it is the λ∥w∥2\lambda \|\mathbf w\|^2λ∥w∥2 form with λ\lambdaλ halved, so the two line vectors from the representer section now cost 1.31.31.3 and 0.0909+0.325=0.41590.0909 + 0.325 = 0.41590.0909+0.325=0.4159. The algorithm had this shape, where [m][m][m] is the positions 1,…,m1, \dots, m1,…,m:

SGD-SoftSVM(S, λ, T):
  θ ← 0
  for t = 1..T:
    w⁽ᵗ⁾ ← θ / (λ t)
    choose i uniformly at random from [m]
    if y_i ⟨w⁽ᵗ⁾, x_i⟩ < 1:
      θ ← θ + y_i x_i
  return w̄ = (1/T) Σ_t w⁽ᵗ⁾

Look at the only thing that ever gets added to θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ: a training vector, times ±1\pm 1±1. Run it on the image sequence, with ψ(xi)\psi(x_i)ψ(xi​) in place of xi\mathbf x_ixi​, and θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ is always a combination of ψ(x1),…,ψ(xm)\psi(x_1), \dots, \psi(x_m)ψ(x1​),…,ψ(xm​), so it can be stored as mmm coefficients. The representer theorem promised that a solution lives in the span; SGD never even leaves it.

So keep two vectors in Rm\mathbb R^mRm, where a superscript (t)(t)(t) marks the value at step ttt: β(t)\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}β(t), the coefficients of θ(t)=∑jβj(t)ψ(xj)\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)} = \sum_j \beta_j^{(t)} \psi(x_j)θ(t)=∑j​βj(t)​ψ(xj​), and α(t)\boldsymbol\alpha^{(t)}α(t), the coefficients of w(t)=∑jαj(t)ψ(xj)\mathbf w^{(t)} = \sum_j \alpha_j^{(t)} \psi(x_j)w(t)=∑j​αj(t)​ψ(xj​).

KernelSGD-SoftSVM(S, K, λ, T):
  β ← 0 ∈ ℝᵐ;  ᾱ ← 0 ∈ ℝᵐ
  for t = 1..T:
    α ← β / (λ t)
    ᾱ ← ᾱ + α / T
    choose i uniformly at random from [m]
    if y_i Σ_j α_j K(x_j, x_i) < 1:
      β_i ← β_i + y_i
  return ᾱ      (predict on x by the sign of Σ_j ᾱ_j K(x_j, x))

Every other coordinate of β\boldsymbol\betaβ stays as it was. The output stands for wˉ=∑jαˉjψ(xj)\bar{\mathbf w} = \sum_j \bar\alpha_j \psi(x_j)wˉ=∑j​αˉj​ψ(xj​), with αˉ=1T∑t=1Tα(t)\bar{\boldsymbol\alpha} = \frac1T \sum_{t=1}^T \boldsymbol\alpha^{(t)}αˉ=T1​∑t=1T​α(t), the bar marking an average over the TTT steps.

[diagram:kernel-sgd: built on the lesson page]

Kernel SGD computes the same hypothesis. Run SGD-SoftSVM on the image sequence and KernelSGD-SoftSVM on SSS with the kernel of ψ\psiψ, using the same random choices of iii. Then the outputs are equal: w^=wˉ\hat{\mathbf w} = \bar{\mathbf w}w^=wˉ, where w^\hat{\mathbf w}w^ is the output of SGD-SoftSVM and wˉ=∑jαˉjψ(xj)\bar{\mathbf w} = \sum_j \bar\alpha_j \psi(x_j)wˉ=∑j​αˉj​ψ(xj​).

Proof. We show by induction on ttt that θ(t)=∑jβj(t)ψ(xj)\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)} = \sum_j \beta_j^{(t)} \psi(x_j)θ(t)=∑j​βj(t)​ψ(xj​) for every ttt.

For t=1t = 1t=1, both sides are 0.

Suppose it holds at step ttt. The two algorithms set w(t)=θ(t)/(λt)\mathbf w^{(t)} = \boldsymbol\theta^{(t)}/(\lambda t)w(t)=θ(t)/(λt) and α(t)=β(t)/(λt)\boldsymbol\alpha^{(t)} = \boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}/(\lambda t)α(t)=β(t)/(λt), so dividing the hypothesis by λt\lambda tλt gives w(t)=∑jαj(t)ψ(xj)\mathbf w^{(t)} = \sum_j \alpha_j^{(t)} \psi(x_j)w(t)=∑j​αj(t)​ψ(xj​). Both pick the same iii. The feature-space test computes

yi⟨w(t),ψ(xi)⟩=yi⟨∑jαj(t)ψ(xj),ψ(xi)⟩=yi∑j=1mαj(t)K(xj,xi),y_i \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \psi(x_i) \rangle = y_i \Big\langle \sum_j \alpha_j^{(t)} \psi(x_j), \psi(x_i) \Big\rangle = y_i \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j^{(t)} K(x_j, x_i),yi​⟨w(t),ψ(xi​)⟩=yi​⟨j∑​αj(t)​ψ(xj​),ψ(xi​)⟩=yi​j=1∑m​αj(t)​K(xj​,xi​),

which is exactly the kernel test, by the same pass-through-the-sum step as in the kernel trick: the two tests compute the same number, so both algorithms take the same branch. If neither updates, both sides of the claim are unchanged. If both update,

θ(t+1)=θ(t)+yiψ(xi)=∑jβj(t)ψ(xj)+yiψ(xi)=∑jβj(t+1)ψ(xj),\boldsymbol\theta^{(t+1)} = \boldsymbol\theta^{(t)} + y_i \psi(x_i) = \sum_{j} \beta_j^{(t)} \psi(x_j) + y_i \psi(x_i) = \sum_j \beta_j^{(t+1)} \psi(x_j),θ(t+1)=θ(t)+yi​ψ(xi​)=j∑​βj(t)​ψ(xj​)+yi​ψ(xi​)=j∑​βj(t+1)​ψ(xj​),

since β(t+1)\boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}β(t+1) differs from β(t)\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}β(t) only by yiy_iyi​ in coordinate iii: adding yiψ(xi)y_i \psi(x_i)yi​ψ(xi​) to θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ is adding yiy_iyi​ to coefficient iii. That completes the induction. It follows that w(t)=∑jαj(t)ψ(xj)\mathbf w^{(t)} = \sum_j \alpha_j^{(t)} \psi(x_j)w(t)=∑j​αj(t)​ψ(xj​) for every ttt, and averaging over ttt, by linearity, w^=1T∑tw(t)=∑jαˉjψ(xj)=wˉ\hat{\mathbf w} = \frac1T \sum_t \mathbf w^{(t)} = \sum_j \bar\alpha_j \psi(x_j) = \bar{\mathbf w}w^=T1​∑t​w(t)=∑j​αˉj​ψ(xj​)=wˉ. ■\blacksquare■

Let’s watch the two runs side by side on the line example, with ψ(x)=(1,x,x2)\psi(x) = (1, x, x^2)ψ(x)=(1,x,x2) and the kernel K(x,x′)=⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩K(x, x') = \langle \psi(x), \psi(x') \rangleK(x,x′)=⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩. One detail matters: the comparison <1< 1<1 is a knife edge, and floating-point rounding can push the two runs to different sides of it when a score lands exactly on 1. Exact fractions remove that doubt. In the snippet, theta follows the feature-space test and beta the kernel test, side by side.

import random
from fractions import Fraction

S = [(x, 1 if abs(x) > 2 else -1) for x in range(-5, 6)]
psi = lambda x: (1, x, x * x)
dot = lambda a, b: sum(i * j for i, j in zip(a, b))
K = lambda x, xp: dot(psi(x), psi(xp))
lam, T, m, rng = Fraction(1, 10), 10_000, len(S), random.Random(0)
theta, beta, ws, alphas = [0, 0, 0], [0] * m, [], []
for t in range(1, T + 1):
    i = rng.randrange(m)
    x, y = S[i]
    ws.append([v / (lam * t) for v in theta])
    alphas.append([v / (lam * t) for v in beta])
    if y * dot(ws[-1], psi(x)) < 1:
        theta = [p + y * q for p, q in zip(theta, psi(x))]
    a = alphas[-1]
    if y * sum(a[j] * K(S[j][0], x) for j in range(m)) < 1:
        beta[i] += y
wbar = [sum(c) / T for c in zip(*ws)]
abar = [sum(c) / T for c in zip(*alphas)]
back = [sum(abar[j] * psi(S[j][0])[c] for j in range(m))
        for c in range(3)]
print(wbar == back, [round(float(v), 4) for v in wbar])

It prints True [-1.3161, -0.0179, 0.2995]: after 10,000 steps, the explicit average weight vector and the one rebuilt from αˉ\bar{\boldsymbol\alpha}αˉ are exactly equal, as fractions. Read the weights as a rule: 0.2995x2−0.0179x−1.3161>00.2995 x^2 - 0.0179 x - 1.3161 > 00.2995x2−0.0179x−1.3161>0 holds roughly when x2>4.4x^2 > 4.4x2>4.4, so it is positive for ∣x∣≥3|x| \ge 3∣x∣≥3 and negative for ∣x∣≤2|x| \le 2∣x∣≤2. The learner found the parabola. (Patience is part of the deal: the average carries SGD’s noisy early steps, and with only 300 steps the same run still mislabels three of the eleven points.)

Cost. Let cKc_KcK​ be the time to evaluate the kernel once: O(n)O(n)O(n) for the polynomial and Gaussian kernels on Rn\mathbb R^nRn, and O(s)O(s)O(s) for subject lines of sss words stored as sets.

  • Time per step. The test needs ∑jαjK(xj,xi)\sum_j \alpha_j K(x_j, x_i)∑j​αj​K(xj​,xi​). Only the coordinates with βj≠0\beta_j \ne 0βj​=0 contribute, and at step ttt at most min⁡(t,m)\min(t, m)min(t,m) of them are nonzero, so the test costs O(min⁡(t,m) cK)O(\min(t, m)\, c_K)O(min(t,m)cK​). Updating αˉ\bar{\boldsymbol\alpha}αˉ the naive way costs O(m)O(m)O(m) per step. Since αˉj=1λT∑tβj(t)/t\bar\alpha_j = \frac{1}{\lambda T} \sum_t \beta_j^{(t)}/tαˉj​=λT1​∑t​βj(t)​/t and βj\beta_jβj​ changes only when example jjj is updated, you can instead settle coordinate jjj lazily at each of its updates, adding its old value times a difference of harmonic numbers (Hn=1+12+⋯+1nH_n = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1nHn​=1+21​+⋯+n1​), ∑t′=t0t−11/t′\sum_{t'=t_0}^{t-1} 1/t'∑t′=t0​t−1​1/t′, which is O(1)O(1)O(1) per update plus O(m)O(m)O(m) at the end. All of TTT steps: O(Tmin⁡(T,m) cK)O(T \min(T, m)\, c_K)O(Tmin(T,m)cK​).
  • With a cached Gram matrix. Precompute all m2m^2m2 kernel values in O(m2cK)O(m^2 c_K)O(m2cK​) time and O(m2)O(m^2)O(m2) space; then each test is O(m)O(m)O(m). For m=16,000m = 16{,}000m=16,000 messages, the Gram matrix has 256 million entries, about 2 GB at 8 bytes each. Caching is a trade, not a free lunch.
  • Space without the cache. O(m)O(m)O(m) for β\boldsymbol\betaβ and αˉ\bar{\boldsymbol\alpha}αˉ, plus the training messages themselves.
  • Prediction. O(r cK)O(r\, c_K)O(rcK​) per new message, where rrr is the number of nonzero αˉj\bar\alpha_jαˉj​, at most mmm.

The lazy formula is easier to trust with numbers. Since αj(t)=βj(t)/(λt)\alpha_j^{(t)} = \beta_j^{(t)}/(\lambda t)αj(t)​=βj(t)​/(λt), averaging gives αˉj=1λT∑t=1Tβj(t)/t\bar\alpha_j = \frac{1}{\lambda T} \sum_{t=1}^T \beta_j^{(t)}/tαˉj​=λT1​∑t=1T​βj(t)​/t: the average coefficient is the history of βj\beta_jβj​, each step divided by its step number. Follow one coordinate for T=6T = 6T=6 steps with λ=0.1\lambda = 0.1λ=0.1, where βj\beta_jβj​ is 0 at step 1, 1 at steps 2 to 4 and 2 at steps 5 and 6. Grouping the steps where it held still gives 1⋅(12+13+14)+2⋅(15+16)1 \cdot (\frac12 + \frac13 + \frac14) + 2 \cdot (\frac15 + \frac16)1⋅(21​+31​+41​)+2⋅(51​+61​), two differences of harmonic numbers:

from fractions import Fraction as F

lam, T = F(1, 10), 6
beta = [0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
direct = sum(b / (lam * t) for t, b in enumerate(beta, 1)) / T
H = lambda a, b: sum(F(1, t) for t in range(a, b + 1))
lazy = (1 * H(2, 4) + 2 * H(5, 6)) / (lam * T)
print(direct, lazy)

It prints 109/36 109/36.

Compare with SGD on explicit features of dimension DDD: O(D)O(D)O(D) per step and O(D)O(D)O(D) space. The kernel version wins whenever DDD is much larger than mmm, which for triples of 50,000 words means always. It does have one cost the explicit version lacks: prediction grows with the number of training messages the hypothesis keeps.

Build it yourself. Using only the Python standard library, with subject lines as sets of word indices (0 winner, 1 claim, 2 verify, 3 password, 4 lunch, 5 meeting, 6 invoice, 7 report):

import itertools
import math
import random

JUNK = [{0, 1, 4}, {2, 3, 4}, {0, 1, 5}, {2, 3, 7}, {0, 1, 2}]
KEEP = [{0, 2, 4}, {1, 3, 4}, {0, 3, 7}, {1, 2, 6},
        {4, 5, 7}, {0, 4, 5}, {3, 6, 7}]
S = ([(frozenset(x), 1) for x in JUNK]
     + [(frozenset(x), -1) for x in KEEP])
ALL = [frozenset(c) for c in itertools.combinations(range(8), 3)]

def label(x):
    return 1 if {0, 1} <= x or {2, 3} <= x else -1

def poly_kernel(a, b, k): ...
def gaussian_kernel(a, b, sigma): ...
def gram(xs, K): ...
def kernel_sgd_svm(S, K, lam, T, rng): ...
def predict(alpha, S, K, x): ...
def train_mistakes(alpha, S, K): ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    K1 = lambda a, b: poly_kernel(a, b, 1)
    K2 = lambda a, b: poly_kernel(a, b, 2)
    assert K2(frozenset({0, 1}), frozenset({1, 2})) == 4
    assert math.isclose(gaussian_kernel(S[0][0], S[3][0], 1.0),
                        math.exp(-3))
    G = gram([x for x, _ in S], K2)
    assert all(G[i][j] == G[j][i]
               for i in range(12) for j in range(12))
    a2 = kernel_sgd_svm(S, K2, 0.0137, 2000, random.Random(0))
    a1 = kernel_sgd_svm(S, K1, 0.0137, 2000, random.Random(0))
    assert train_mistakes(a2, S, K2) == 0
    assert train_mistakes(a1, S, K1) >= 1
    assert round(sum(a2), 4) == -0.3
    unseen = [predict(a2, S, K2, x) != label(x) for x in ALL]
    assert sum(unseen) == 3
  1. Implement the six functions. poly_kernel is (1+∣a∩b∣)k(1 + |a \cap b|)^k(1+∣a∩b∣)k and gaussian_kernel is e−∣a△b∣/(2σ)e^{-|a \triangle b|/(2\sigma)}e−∣a△b∣/(2σ), the set forms of the two kernels from earlier. kernel_sgd_svm follows KernelSGD-SoftSVM exactly: at each step, first compute α\boldsymbol\alphaα and add α/T\boldsymbol\alpha/Tα/T to αˉ\bar{\boldsymbol\alpha}αˉ, then draw i = rng.randrange(m), then test and update. Return αˉ\bar{\boldsymbol\alpha}αˉ as a list. predict returns +1+1+1 when ∑jαˉjK(xj,x)>0\sum_j \bar\alpha_j K(x_j, x) > 0∑j​αˉj​K(xj​,x)>0 and −1-1−1 otherwise.
  2. The odd λ=0.0137\lambda = 0.0137λ=0.0137 is on purpose. With a round value such as 0.1, some step lands exactly on the boundary yi∑jαjK(xj,xi)=1y_i \sum_j \alpha_j K(x_j, x_i) = 1yi​∑j​αj​K(xj​,xi​)=1, and the order in which your code adds floating-point numbers decides the branch. Try 0.1 and see whether your sum(a2) still matches.
  3. Why must train_mistakes(a1, S, K1) be at least 1, whatever the learner does? Find the four messages in S that make it so.
  4. Train with the Gaussian kernel for σ∈{0.25,1,4}\sigma \in \{0.25, 1, 4\}σ∈{0.25,1,4} and count mistakes on ALL. Which σ\sigmaσ does worst, and why, in terms of what “close” means?
  5. Replace the cached Gram matrix by kernel evaluations only for the nonzero βj\beta_jβj​, and time both versions for m=2,000m = 2{,}000m=2,000 random subject lines.

How many labels? Margins in feature space

The kernel trick solved the computational half of the bug. Now the statistical half: is it reasonable to learn in a feature space with over a billion coordinates from a budget of labels you can afford? Lesson 15b gave the tool, and it transfers to kernels without a change.

Recall it. Let every message satisfy ∥ψ(x)∥≤ρ\|\psi(x)\| \le \rho∥ψ(x)∥≤ρ, so ρ\rhoρ is lesson 15b’s radius, and let A(S)A(S)A(S) be the solution of soft-SVM, min⁡wλ∥w∥2+LShinge(w)\min_{\mathbf w} \lambda \|\mathbf w\|^2 + L^{\text{hinge}}_S(\mathbf w)minw​λ∥w∥2+LShinge​(w), on the image sequence. Then for every vector u\mathbf uu in the feature space,

ES∼Dm[LD0−1(A(S))]≤LDhinge(u)+λ∥u∥2+2ρ2λm.\mathop{\mathbb E}_{S \sim \mathcal D^m}\big[ L^{0-1}_{\mathcal D}(A(S)) \big] \le L^{\text{hinge}}_{\mathcal D}(\mathbf u) + \lambda \|\mathbf u\|^2 + \frac{2\rho^2}{\lambda m}.ES∼Dm​[LD0−1​(A(S))]≤LDhinge​(u)+λ∥u∥2+λm2ρ2​.

Read it from the inside out.

  • A(S)A(S)A(S) is the hypothesis soft-SVM returns on the training sequence SSS, and LD0−1(A(S))L^{0-1}_{\mathcal D}(A(S))LD0−1​(A(S)) is its true risk with the 0-1 loss: the probability it mislabels a fresh message.
  • Under E\mathbb EE, “the average value of”, S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm says the training sequence is mmm examples drawn i.i.d. from D\mathcal DD, so the average runs over lucky and unlucky archives alike.
  • On the right, LDhinge(u)L^{\text{hinge}}_{\mathcal D}(\mathbf u)LDhinge​(u) is the expected hinge loss of a comparison vector u\mathbf uu, λ∥u∥2\lambda \|\mathbf u\|^2λ∥u∥2 its penalty, and 2ρ2λm\frac{2\rho^2}{\lambda m}λm2ρ2​ a price that falls as the number of labels mmm grows.

In plain words: on average, the filter’s error rate is at most any comparison vector’s hinge loss, plus its penalty, plus a term that shrinks with more labels. Suppose a separator u\mathbf uu with norm BBB has y⟨u,ψ(x)⟩≥1y \langle \mathbf u, \psi(x) \rangle \ge 1y⟨u,ψ(x)⟩≥1 on every message. Every hinge loss of u\mathbf uu is then max⁡{0,1−y⟨u,ψ(x)⟩}=0\max\{0, 1 - y\langle \mathbf u, \psi(x) \rangle\} = 0max{0,1−y⟨u,ψ(x)⟩}=0, so

E[LD0−1(A(S))]≤λB2+2ρ2λm.\mathop{\mathbb E}\big[ L^{0-1}_{\mathcal D}(A(S)) \big] \le \lambda B^2 + \frac{2\rho^2}{\lambda m}.E[LD0−1​(A(S))]≤λB2+λm2ρ2​.

Which λ\lambdaλ makes the right side smallest? For positive numbers aaa and bbb, a+b≥2aba + b \ge 2\sqrt{ab}a+b≥2ab​, because a+b−2ab=(a−b)2≥0a + b - 2\sqrt{ab} = (\sqrt a - \sqrt b)^2 \ge 0a+b−2ab​=(a​−b​)2≥0, with equality when a=ba = ba=b. Here ab=λB2⋅2ρ2λm=2ρ2B2mab = \lambda B^2 \cdot \frac{2\rho^2}{\lambda m} = \frac{2\rho^2 B^2}{m}ab=λB2⋅λm2ρ2​=m2ρ2B2​, whatever λ\lambdaλ is, so the right side is at least 22ρ2B2/m2\sqrt{2\rho^2 B^2/m}22ρ2B2/m​, and setting λB2=2ρ2λm\lambda B^2 = \frac{2\rho^2}{\lambda m}λB2=λm2ρ2​, that is λ=2ρ2/(B2m)\lambda = \sqrt{2\rho^2/(B^2 m)}λ=2ρ2/(B2m)​, achieves it:

E[LD0−1(A(S))]≤8ρ2B2m.\mathop{\mathbb E}\big[ L^{0-1}_{\mathcal D}(A(S)) \big] \le \sqrt{\frac{8 \rho^2 B^2}{m}}.E[LD0−1​(A(S))]≤m8ρ2B2​​.

In plain words: the expected error shrinks like one over the square root of the number of labels, at a rate set by ρB\rho BρB. No dimension anywhere. To guarantee an expected true risk of at most ε\varepsilonε, the error rate you are willing to accept, solve 8ρ2B2/m≤ε\sqrt{8\rho^2B^2/m} \le \varepsilon8ρ2B2/m​≤ε for mmm: it is enough that m≥8ρ2B2/ε2m \ge 8\rho^2 B^2/\varepsilon^2m≥8ρ2B2/ε2. And both quantities can be read through the kernel: ρ2=max⁡xK(x,x)\rho^2 = \max_x K(x, x)ρ2=maxx​K(x,x), the largest squared length ∥ψ(x)∥2\|\psi(x)\|^2∥ψ(x)∥2 over all messages, and a separator written as u=∑iγiψ(zi)\mathbf u = \sum_i \gamma_i \psi(z_i)u=∑i​γi​ψ(zi​) has B2=∑i,jγiγjK(zi,zj)B^2 = \sum_{i,j} \gamma_i \gamma_j K(z_i, z_j)B2=∑i,j​γi​γj​K(zi​,zj​). As in lesson 9a, any separator with margin 1 everywhere is a certificate: its norm bounds the labels you need. You never need the best one, just one you can check.

Now the mail. For the degree-2 polynomial kernel on three-word subject lines, K(x,x)=(1+3)2=16K(x, x) = (1 + 3)^2 = 16K(x,x)=(1+3)2=16, so ρ=4\rho = 4ρ=4; that was the 16 printed earlier. And the hand-built u\mathbf uu is a certificate with B2=5B^2 = 5B2=5. Push them through: with m=16,000m = 16{,}000m=16,000, the best λ\lambdaλ is 2⋅16/(5⋅16,000)=0.02\sqrt{2 \cdot 16/(5 \cdot 16{,}000)} = 0.022⋅16/(5⋅16,000)​=0.02, the two terms λB2\lambda B^2λB2 and 2ρ2/(λm)2\rho^2/(\lambda m)2ρ2/(λm) are both 0.1, and their sum is the bound 0.2:

import math

rho, B, m = 4, math.sqrt(5), 16_000
lam = math.sqrt(2 * rho ** 2 / (B ** 2 * m))
terms = [lam * B ** 2, 2 * rho ** 2 / (lam * m)]
print(round(lam, 4), [round(t, 4) for t in terms],
      round(sum(terms), 4),
      round(math.sqrt(8 * rho ** 2 * B ** 2 / m), 4))

It prints 0.02 [0.1, 0.1] 0.2 0.2. What about degree kkk? On 0/1 vectors a word times itself is itself, so the monomial x1x2x_1 x_2x1​x2​ appears in every coordinate whose index tuple uses exactly the indices 1 and 2, padded with zeros or repeats. Counting the kkk-tuples over {0,1,2}\{0, 1, 2\}{0,1,2} that contain both a 1 and a 2 by inclusion and exclusion gives ck=3k−2⋅2k+1c_k = 3^k - 2 \cdot 2^k + 1ck​=3k−2⋅2k+1: all 3k3^k3k lists, minus the 2k2^k2k that miss 1 and the 2k2^k2k that miss 2, plus the all-zeros list, which was taken away twice. For k=2k = 2k=2, 9−8+1=29 - 8 + 1 = 29−8+1=2: the lists (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) and (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1). The snippet’s c is this count. Spread a weight of 2/ck2/c_k2/ck​ over those coordinates, the same for x3x4x_3 x_4x3​x4​, and put −1-1−1 on the all-zero tuple: the score is still 2x1x2+2x3x4−12x_1x_2 + 2x_3x_4 - 12x1​x2​+2x3​x4​−1, and the squared norm is 1+2⋅ck(2/ck)2=1+8/ck1 + 2 \cdot c_k (2/c_k)^2 = 1 + 8/c_k1+2⋅ck​(2/ck​)2=1+8/ck​. Meanwhile ρ2=(1+3)k\rho^2 = (1 + 3)^kρ2=(1+3)k grows. The labels needed for ε=0.2\varepsilon = 0.2ε=0.2:

import math

s, eps = 3, 0.2

def labels(rho_B):
    return math.ceil(8 * rho_B ** 2 / eps ** 2)

for k in (2, 3, 4):
    c = 3 ** k - 2 * 2 ** k + 1
    B = math.sqrt(1 + 8 / c)
    rho = (1 + s) ** (k / 2)
    print(k, c, round(B, 3), round(rho * B, 3), labels(rho * B))

It prints 2 2 2.236 8.944 16000, 3 12 1.291 10.328 21334 and 4 50 1.077 17.233 59392. Degree 2 certifies an expected true risk of at most 0.2 with 16,000 labels. Higher degrees have smaller certificates BBB but a larger radius ρ\rhoρ, and the product grows. A richer kernel is not a free upgrade.

Two things about these numbers. First, compare them with counting dimensions. Halfspaces over pairs of a 50,000-word vocabulary live in a space of about 1.25×1091.25 \times 10^91.25×109 dimensions, so a guarantee that grows with the VC dimension, like those of lesson 6a, needs labels in proportion to that. The margin certificate does not mention the vocabulary at all: 16,000 labels for 1,000 words, 50,000 words or a million. Second, the guarantee is an upper bound in expectation, and a loose one. The filter will usually do far better than 0.2; what the bound gives you is a promise you can make before you train, the kind operations asked for in lesson 9a.

One honest caveat. The bound is about the exact soft-SVM solution, and KernelSGD-SoftSVM approximates it, with an optimization error that lesson 14a showed shrinks as the number of steps TTT grows. In the lab, TTT is large enough for that gap to be small, but it is not part of the certificate.

Fix the bug

Time to ship. In the lab below, the filter reads three-word subject lines from a vocabulary of 1,000 words, and this month’s junk is marked by winner with claim, or verify with password. The archive holds 20,000 labelled subject lines, which is your label budget. You choose a kernel (linear, polynomial of degree 2, 3 or 4, or Gaussian with a choice of σ\sigmaσ) and how many labels to use. The lab sets λ\lambdaλ from the bound and trains KernelSGD-SoftSVM.

The goal is a filter whose expected true risk is certified to be at most 0.2 by the margin bound, using a certificate the lab can check, within the budget, and whose measured error on fresh subject lines agrees. A filter that happens to do well without a certificate does not count: next month’s junk will not ask whether you were lucky.

Before you train, work out each kernel’s label count from the table above, and ask what the linear kernel can possibly certify. For the Gaussian kernel, think about the three subject lines from “Kernels are prior knowledge” before you trust it.

[lab-act2: built on the lesson page]

What people get wrong

“The kernel trick makes the feature space small.” The feature space is exactly as large as before, possibly infinite. What shrinks is what you store and compute: mmm coefficients and mmm training messages instead of a weight vector, and kernel values instead of coordinates. The price moves to mmm: the Gram matrix has m2m^2m2 entries and each prediction touches up to mmm training messages.

“Any similarity function is a kernel.” Only the positive semidefinite ones. max⁡{x,x′}\max\{x, x'\}max{x,x′} looks like a perfectly reasonable similarity and fails on two points. Plug a non-kernel into soft-SVM and the “norm” α⊤Gα\boldsymbol\alpha^\top G \boldsymbol\alphaα⊤Gα can go negative; the objective is then no longer the problem you meant, and every guarantee you derived for it is gone.

“A Gaussian kernel can separate anything, so it is the safe default.” With a small enough σ\sigmaσ, the Gram matrix of distinct messages is close to the identity and any labelling is separable. That is exactly the memorizer of lesson 1 in a new coat: separable with a norm that grows with the number of messages, so the margin bound needs more labels than there are messages (the first concept-check question asks you to show it). The kernel is prior knowledge, and the wrong prior costs labels.

“The representer theorem says the solution uses only a few training messages.” It says the solution is a combination of the training messages, possibly all mmm of them. Which coefficients are zero depends on the loss; for hard-SVM, lesson 15b’s support vectors are the ones that remain.

Recap and the next bug

  1. An embedding ψ\psiψ sends messages into a feature space where a halfspace can express nonlinear rules, such as “winner and claim both appear”. The true risk is preserved: LDψ(h)=LD(h∘ψ)L_{\mathcal D_\psi}(h) = L_{\mathcal D}(h \circ \psi)LDψ​​(h)=LD​(h∘ψ).
  2. The representer theorem: whenever the objective sees w\mathbf ww only through ⟨w,ψ(xi)⟩\langle \mathbf w, \psi(x_i) \rangle⟨w,ψ(xi​)⟩ plus a nondecreasing function of ∥w∥\|\mathbf w\|∥w∥, some optimal w\mathbf ww is a combination ∑iαiψ(xi)\sum_i \alpha_i \psi(x_i)∑i​αi​ψ(xi​) of the training vectors.
  3. The kernel trick: rewritten in α\boldsymbol\alphaα, learning and prediction need only the kernel K(x,x′)=⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩K(x, x') = \langle \psi(x), \psi(x') \rangleK(x,x′)=⟨ψ(x),ψ(x′)⟩, through the Gram matrix. The polynomial kernel (1+⟨x,x′⟩)k(1 + \langle \mathbf x, \mathbf x' \rangle)^k(1+⟨x,x′⟩)k costs O(n)O(n)O(n) for a space of (n+1)k(n+1)^k(n+1)k coordinates; the Gaussian kernel costs O(n)O(n)O(n) for an infinite one.
  4. A kernel is prior knowledge: the polynomial kernel believes in combinations of words, the Gaussian kernel in nearness, the substring kernel in signatures.
  5. A symmetric KKK is a kernel exactly when every Gram matrix is positive semidefinite.
  6. KernelSGD-SoftSVM stores β∈Rm\boldsymbol\beta \in \mathbb R^mβ∈Rm instead of θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ and computes exactly the same hypothesis as SGD in the feature space. In lesson 10a, boosting handled a huge feature space with a weak learner that hands it one good coordinate at a time; kernels handle it by never needing coordinates at all.
  7. The margin bound 8ρ2B2/m\sqrt{8 \rho^2 B^2/m}8ρ2B2/m​ does not depend on the dimension, and any separator with margin 1 is a certificate for it.

Your filter is catching the pair-marked junk again, and the certificate is pinned above your desk. Then the product team walks over with a survey. Users are grateful, they say, but junk or keep is not what they actually want. They want their mail sorted into folders: work, personal, promotions and junk. And within the inbox, they want the important messages first. A single yes/no filter cannot do either: it has two answers, and folders need four, while an ordering needs a score for every message that is right relative to the others. Can the halfspaces, margins and kernels you have built answer questions with more than two answers? That is the next lesson: multiclass, ranking and complex prediction problems.
